The '''Ruth Lyttle Satter Prize in Mathematics''', also called the '''Satter Prize''', is one of twenty-one prizes given out by the [[American Mathematical Society]] (AMS).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ams.org/profession/prizes-awards/prizes#tab2 |title=Prizes and Awards |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |access-date=September 14, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007182945/http://www.ams.org/prizes-awards/palist.cgi#tab2 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> It is presented biennially in recognition of an outstanding contribution to mathematics research by a woman in the previous six years.<ref name="ams">{{cite web |title=Ruth Lyttle Satter Prize in Mathematics |url=http://www.ams.org/profession/prizes-awards/ams-prizes/satter-prize |access-date=September 13, 2017 |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240723121106/http://www.ams.org/prizes-awards/paview.cgi?parent_id=35 |archive-date=July 23, 2024}}</ref> The award was funded in 1990 using a donation from [[Joan Birman]], in memory of her sister, [[Ruth Lyttle Satter]],{{sfn|Case|Leggett|2005|p=97}} who worked primarily in biological sciences, and was a proponent for equal opportunities for women in science.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.awis.affiniscape.com/displaycommon.cfm?an=1&subarticlenbr=61 |title=Educational Awards: Ruth Satter |publisher=[[Association for Women in Science]] |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130102015633/http://www.awis.affiniscape.com/displaycommon.cfm?an=1&subarticlenbr=61 |archive-date=January 2, 2013 |access-date=September 14, 2017 |url-status=dead  }}</ref> First awarded in 1991, the award is intended to "honor [Satter's] commitment to research and to encourage women in science".<ref name="j2017">{{cite journal |date=April 2017 |title=2017 Ruth Lyttle Satter Prize |url=http://www.ams.org/publications/journals/notices/201704/rnoti-p316.pdf |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |volume=64 |issue=4 |page=316}}</ref>  The winner is selected by the council of the AMS, based on the recommendation of a selection committee.<ref name="j2017"/> 

== Award details and history ==
The prize is awarded at the [[Joint Mathematics Meetings]] during odd numbered years, and has always carried a modest cash reward. Since 2003, the prize has been [[United States dollar|$]]5,000,<ref name="j2017" /><ref>{{cite journal |date=April 2003 |title=2003 Satter Prize |url=http://www.ams.org/notices/200304/comm-satter.pdf |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |volume=50 |issue=4 |pages=474–475}}</ref> while from 1997 to 2001, the prize came with $1,200,<ref name="j2001" /><ref>{{cite journal |date=March 1997 |title=1997 Satter Prize |url=http://www.ams.org/notices/199703/comm-satter.pdf |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |volume=44 |issue=3 |pages=348–349}}</ref> and $4,000 prior to that.<ref>{{cite journal |date=April 1995 |title=1995 Satter Prize |url=http://www.ams.org/notices/199504/prize-satter.pdf |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |volume=42 |issue=4 |pages=459–460}}</ref> If a joint award is given, the prize money is split between the recipients.<ref name="j2001" />

[[Dusa McDuff]] was the first recipient of the award, for her work on [[symplectic geometry]].{{sfn|Morrow|Perl|1998|p=140}} A joint award was given for the first time in 2001, when [[Karen E. Smith]] and [[Sijue Wu]] shared the award.<ref name="j2001">{{cite journal |date=April 2001 |title=2001 Ruth Lyttle Satter Prize |url=http://www.ams.org/notices/200104/comm-satter.pdf |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |volume=48 |issue=4 |pages=411–412}}</ref> The 2013 prize winner was [[Maryam Mirzakhani]], who, the following year, became the first woman to be awarded the [[Fields Medal]], which is considered to be the highest honor a mathematician can receive.<ref>{{cite news |date=August 22, 2006 |title=Reclusive Russian turns down math world's highest honour |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/reclusive-russian-turns-down-math-world-s-highest-honour-1.622524 |access-date=September 13, 2017 |website=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] |agency=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-40617094 |title=Maryam Mirzakhani, first woman to win maths' Fields Medal, dies |website=[[BBC News]] |date=July 15, 2017 |access-date=September 13, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231208192709/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-40617094 |archive-date=December 8, 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> She won both awards for her work on "the geometry of Riemann surfaces and their moduli spaces".<ref>{{cite news |url=https://thewire.in/158018/maryam-mirzakhani-fields-medal-rouhani/ |title=Maryam Mirzakhani, First Woman and Iranian to Win Fields Medal, Dies at 40 |website=[[The Wire (Indian web publication)|The Wire]] |date=July 15, 2017 |access-date=September 13, 2017 |archive-date=July 15, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170715133128/https://thewire.in/158018/maryam-mirzakhani-fields-medal-rouhani/ |url-status=live}}</ref> The most recent winner is [[Ana Caraiani]], who was awarded the prize in 2025 "for contributions to arithmetic geometry and number theory: in particular, the Langlands program.".<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 22, 2024 |title=Caraiani to Receive 2025 AMS Satter Prize |url=https://www.ams.org/news?news_id=7377 |access-date=October 22, 2024 |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |archive-date=November 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241107124753/https://www.ams.org/news?news_id=7377 |url-status=live}}</ref>
